Yes. Absolute productivity advantages do not rule out mutual gains. What matters is comparative advantage: each country should specialize in the good for which its opportunity cost is lower (even if it is absolutely less productive at both), then trade. If relative productivities differ, both can consume more of both goods than under autarky.

CONFIDENCE: 95

US importers legally pay the tariff to the US government at the border. Economic evidence (especially from the 2018–2019 tariffs) shows nearly complete pass-through into higher US import prices, so the cost is borne mostly by American firms and consumers rather than by foreign exporters lowering their prices.

CONFIDENCE: 85

Yes. Vaccination routinely generates positive externalities that private decisions do not fully internalize, so the social return exceeds the private return and unsubsidized, voluntary uptake is typically too low.

When one person is vaccinated, the probability that others are infected falls (directly via reduced transmission, and indirectly once coverage approaches a herd-immunity threshold). Those benefits—avoided medical spending, avoided productivity losses, and avoided disruption from outbreaks—accrue largely to other people and to public budgets. Standard externality theory therefore implies a Pigouvian subsidy (or an equivalent public purchase/free provision) equal to the marginal external benefit. Where transaction costs, free-riding, or behavioral frictions make price instruments insufficient to reach the coverage level that minimizes total social cost, a requirement can be the lower-cost instrument; the economic justification is the same externality, not a separate medical claim.

Empirical cost-benefit work is consistent with this logic. Childhood immunization programs, seasonal influenza vaccination, and several outbreak vaccines show benefit-cost ratios well above 1 even when only monetized medical costs and lost work time are counted; including epidemic-prevention benefits widens the gap further. The case is disease- and context-specific (waning immunity, adverse-event rates, and baseline transmission all matter), but the existence of a substantial economic rationale for subsidy or requirement in many real vaccination programs is not in serious doubt.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Cities that introduced congestion pricing (London, Stockholm, and Singapore) have generally found that it cuts traffic volumes and congestion in the charged zones—often on the order of 15–25% during priced periods—while raising travel speeds, shifting some trips to transit or off-peak times, modestly improving air quality, and raising revenue that can fund transport. Pre-launch opposition is common, but acceptance usually rises once those effects are visible; broader business impacts have tended to be small or neutral rather than sharply negative.

CONFIDENCE: 86

Yes. Phasing out leaded gasoline (largely complete in the United States by the mid-1990s, and later elsewhere) and restricting lead paint (residential use banned in the US in 1978) produced large, well-documented net benefits.

Lead is a potent neurotoxin with no known safe exposure level for children. Before regulation, gasoline and deteriorating paint were the dominant sources of population exposure. After the phase-outs, average US blood-lead levels in children fell by more than 90 percent (from roughly 15 µg/dL in the late 1970s to under 1 µg/dL today). That decline tracks the regulatory timeline far more closely than other social or economic changes.

The health gains are not speculative. Lower lead exposure is causally linked to higher IQ, better school performance, fewer behavioral and attention problems, and reduced cardiovascular and kidney disease later in life. Economic valuations that monetize avoided IQ loss, special-education costs, crime, and medical care routinely find benefits in the hundreds of billions of dollars—orders of magnitude above the compliance costs of reformulating fuel and switching to lead-free paint. EPA retrospective analyses of the Clean Air Act reach the same conclusion for the lead provisions specifically.

The lead–crime correlation (childhood exposure in the 1950s–1970s predicting crime rates 20 years later) is consistent with the toxicology and with international patterns, though it is not required to establish net benefit; the cognitive and health effects alone suffice. Residual lead in soil and old housing remains a problem, but that is an argument for further remediation, not evidence that the original phase-outs were mistaken.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Strict rent control (binding caps that prevent rents from tracking market levels, often with vacancy control) has been studied extensively in empirical economics. The central findings are:

- It lowers rents and raises tenure length for incumbent tenants in controlled units, transferring wealth from landlords to those tenants in the short run.
- It reduces the supply of rental housing. Landlords convert units to owner-occupancy, condos, or other uses, delay or cancel maintenance and improvements, and developers build less new rental stock. Studies of San Francisco, Cambridge (MA), and other cities find sizable losses in the rental stock (on the order of 15% in the San Francisco case) and lower housing quality.
- It misallocates housing: households stay in units that no longer match their size or location needs because moving means losing the controlled rent, which lowers mobility and leaves shortages for newcomers.
- Spillovers often raise rents and reduce availability in the uncontrolled sector, so later arrivals and lower-income outsiders bear much of the cost. Property values of nearby uncontrolled buildings can also suffer from neglected controlled stock.

Economists’ consensus, across multiple cities and designs, is that these supply, quality, and allocation effects dominate, so strict rent control worsens a city’s overall housing-market outcomes even while helping sitting tenants.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Occupational licensing (government-mandated credentials, training hours, exams, or fees to work in a trade) has been studied extensively in labor economics. The best-documented effects, especially for lower-risk occupations such as barbers, cosmetologists, florists, and many contractor categories, are:

- **Higher earnings for licensed workers and higher prices for consumers.** By restricting entry, licensing reduces labor supply. Estimates commonly put the wage premium in the range of roughly 10–15 percent; consumer prices rise correspondingly.
- **Lower employment and fewer practitioners.** Barriers (time, tuition, exam failure, fees) keep people out of the occupation, including people who would otherwise provide the service.
- **Little consistent gain in quality or safety.** Across multiple studies of barbering, cosmetology, floristry, and similar fields, measurable improvements in service quality, complaint rates, or consumer outcomes are weak, null, or absent once other factors are controlled. Effects are more mixed for higher-risk trades (e.g., some electrical or plumbing work), but even there the quality benefits are often small relative to the costs.
- **Reduced geographic mobility.** Because rules differ sharply by state, licensing makes it harder for workers to move and continue practicing, lowering labor-market flexibility.
- **Disparate barriers to entry.** The requirements tend to fall more heavily on lower-income people, immigrants, and those with criminal records, narrowing opportunity without clear offsetting public-safety gains in the occupations cited.

These patterns appear in work by researchers such as Morris Kleiner and in summaries from the Obama White House Council of Economic Advisers, Federal Trade Commission, and multiple state-level audits. Net effects are therefore usually described as transfers to incumbents plus deadweight loss, rather than clear improvements in consumer welfare.

CONFIDENCE: 82

The statutory (legal) burden of the corporate income tax falls on corporations, but the economic burden is shifted and shared. In standard open-economy models with mobile capital, the tax reduces the return to investment; capital relocates until after-tax returns equalize, which lowers the domestic capital stock, labor productivity, and wages. Owners of capital (shareholders and other capital owners, including those outside the corporate sector) therefore bear part of the burden through lower returns, while workers bear part through lower wages. A smaller share can also fall on consumers via higher output prices when firms have market power, but this channel is generally secondary.

Exact shares are not settled and depend on capital mobility, openness, and time horizon. Closed-economy models (e.g., Harberger) assign essentially the entire long-run burden to capital. Open-economy estimates and official distributional assumptions commonly used by the CBO and JCT place roughly 20–50% (often ~25%) on labor and the rest on capital; some empirical studies find larger labor shares. Short-run incidence falls more heavily on existing shareholders because capital is less mobile in the near term.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Moderate city-level minimum-wage increases of roughly 10–15% produce little or no detectable decline in overall employment. High-quality quasi-experimental studies (border-discontinuity designs, bunching estimators, and synthetic controls) consistently find employment elasticities near zero for the workers whose wages are directly raised; any hours reductions that appear are small and concentrated among the lowest-skilled teens or in a minority of studies. Earnings of low-wage workers therefore rise, and the simple competitive prediction of large job losses is not borne out for increases of this size.

CONFIDENCE: 72
